svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 3. What leaves the device, and who holds the key to it
svg.desc: Three tiers describing where mobile data ends up. In the first tier data never leaves the handset. In the second it is synchronised to a cloud account and encrypted with a key the vendor also holds, so it is reachable by a legal request, by a breach of the provider, or by a change of policy. In the third it is synchronised but encrypted with a key only the user holds. A panel below shows that the third tier is not a permanent property of a product: one vendor's strongest option was withdrawn for users in one country in February 2025 following a government demand, remains unavailable there in September 2026, and is the subject of continuing litigation. A closing band gives the two settings on each platform that move the most data between tiers.
svg.text: Figure 3: What Leaves the Device, and Who Holds the Key
Your handset is largely a client for a cloud account. Which tier your data sits in decides what a legal request or a breach reaches.
TIER 1
it never leaves
On the handset only
Nothing to request, nothing to breach, nothing to hand over. The cost is that a lost device is a lost copy, so this tier needs its own
backup discipline: an encrypted local backup you actually restore from occasionally.
TIER 2
they hold a key
as well as you
Synchronised, and the provider can decrypt it
This is the default on both platforms for most categories, and it is where the great majority of people's photographs, messages and backups live.
Reachable three ways: a lawful request, a breach of the provider, and a change of policy you were not consulted about.
A backup in this tier can also expose a conversation that was end to end encrypted in transit, because the backup holds the plain text.
TIER 3
only you hold it
Synchronised, and only you can decrypt it
Available on both platforms as an option, and switched off by default on the one where it is most discussed. It moves most of Tier 2 up here in
one setting, and it hands you the lockout risk from Lesson 4.4 in exchange, which is a trade worth making deliberately rather than by accident.
Tier 3 is not a permanent property of a product, and here is the proof
In February 2025 one vendor withdrew its strongest encryption option for users in a single country, rather than comply with a government demand for access.
New users there cannot switch it on. Existing users were required to switch it off. As of September 2026 it has still not been restored, the original worldwide
demand was withdrawn but a narrower one replaced it, and the matter remains in litigation more than eighteen months later.
The lesson is not about one company. It is that "we cannot read your data" is a statement about the current product in your current country.
The two settings that move the most data between tiers, on either platform

g.text: The device backup. It is the single largest object you own and it usually contains everything else, including message histories. Check which tier it is in first.
Photograph synchronisation. The largest volume, the richest metadata, and the category people most often forget is on. Lesson 1.3 explains why photographs matter.

svg.text: Sort your own data into these three tiers before choosing a platform. Most people discover the tiers are not where they assumed.
